items.text: If you keep bubbling the carbon dioxide through the limewater, the white precipitate will eventually disappear again. This is because the CO2 reacts with the calcium carbonate to form calcium hydrogencarbonate, which is soluble in water:

items.label: text
items.text: Safety Note: Wear eye protection. Avoid inhaling or 'sniffing' chlorine or ammonia, especially if you have a breathing problem such as asthma.

items.label: text
items.text: A lighted splint is held to the mouth of the tube. The hydrogen explodes with a squeaky pop.

items.label: text
items.text: The hydrogen combines explosively with oxygen in the air to make water.

items.label: text
items.text: A glowing splint is put into the tube containing the gas. Oxygen relights a glowing splint.

items.label: section_header
items.text: THE TEST FOR CARBON DIOXIDE GAS

items.label: text
items.text: The carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater. Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky/chalky/cloudy.

items.label: text
items.text: Limewater is calcium hydroxide solution. Carbon dioxide reacts with it to form a white precipitate of calcium carbonate.

items.label: text
items.text: A piece of damp litmus paper or universal indicator paper is put into the testtube or held over its mouth. Chlorine is a green gas that bleaches (turns white) the damp litmus paper or universal indicator paper.

items.label: text
items.text: If blue litmus paper or universal indicator paper are used for this test, they go red first (the chlorine dissolves in the water to form an acidic solution) and then white.
